featured.summary: In 2006 an inquiry issued 23 recommendations. Four months later, Canada apologized to Maher Arar.

cases.title: The Arar inquiry
cases.question: What led Canada to apologize to Maher Arar?
cases.summary: An inquiry traced how Canadian agencies handled information about Maher Arar. Four months after its findings appeared, the federal government apologized and announced a settlement.

sources.title: Report of the events relating to Maher Arar
sources.publisher: Commission of Inquiry into the Actions of Canadian Officials in Relation to Maher Arar

sources.title: Commissioner O’Connor’s findings
Letter of apology and announcement of settlement

timeline.title: Detention and removal
timeline.text: US authorities detained Arar in New York and sent him to Syria via Jordan. He returned to Canada in 2003.

timeline.title: The inquiry reports
timeline.text: Commissioner Dennis O’Connor published findings on Canadian officials’ conduct and made 23 recommendations.

timeline.title: Canada apologizes
timeline.text: The prime minister issued a written apology to Arar and his family and announced the conclusion of mediation.

finding.text: O’Connor found no evidence that Arar had committed an offence or posed a threat to Canadian security. He considered it very likely that US authorities relied on information the RCMP supplied.

outcome.text: Canada accepted all 23 recommendations. It announced a settlement of CAD $10.5 million plus legal costs.

limits.text: US authorities did not participate in the inquiry. The commissioner could not determine exactly how they made the removal decision.

cases.title: Canada’s NATO oral histories
cases.question: What does a declassified interview add to a signed treaty?
cases.summary: Compare what Canada signed in 1949 with a diplomat’s later account of the negotiations. The Canada Declassified exhibit brings the original interviews into public view.

sources.title: The North Atlantic Treaty
In Alliance oral history exhibit
Interview with Escott Reid
In Alliance, digitized volume

timeline.title: The treaty is signed
timeline.text: Canada and the other founding parties signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington. Article 2 includes international economic cooperation.

timeline.title: Participants record their memories
timeline.text: Roger Hill recorded interviews with Canadian diplomats, officials and military officers. Escott Reid recounted Canada’s part in the early alliance.

timeline.title: The interviews are compiled
timeline.text: The Global Affairs Canada library holds a digitized edition of the resulting oral history volume.

finding.text: Read Reid’s interview alongside Article 2. The transcript preserves his account of the negotiations, while the signed text records the wording the parties adopted.

outcome.text: The university exhibit says the interviews were declassified under Canada’s Access to Information Act. It organizes thirteen interviews for public reading.

limits.text: The exhibit gives the recording period but does not specify the declassification date. A retrospective account also leaves other participants’ recollections open.

connection.title: Find federal access-request summaries
connection.text: Search completed Canadian access requests for leads to other federal records.

cases.title: The Brown & Williamson documents
cases.question: How did an unsolicited box of papers become a public research archive?
cases.summary: A tobacco company challenged public access to its internal documents at the University of California. The university’s collection and a later industry settlement preserve two distinct routes to disclosure.

sources.title: UCSF Brown & Williamson Collection
History of the Industry Documents Library
Smoking and Health Proposal, original memorandum
The Master Settlement Agreement, twenty years later

timeline.title: A box reaches UCSF
timeline.text: An anonymous source sent internal Brown & Williamson documents to a UCSF professor. Copies went to the university’s Tobacco Control Archives.

timeline.title: The library faces a lawsuit
timeline.text: Brown & Williamson sought removal of the papers. The court allowed public access at the library.

timeline.title: A separate settlement is reached
timeline.text: Forty-six states, the District of Columbia and five US territories reached the Master Settlement Agreement with four major tobacco manufacturers.

finding.text: In a related original memorandum, the company proposed making doubt about smoking and health central to its public communications. The document records a proposed strategy.

outcome.text: Researchers gained access to the disputed collection. UCSF’s guide describes the legal challenge and offers a route to the documents themselves.

limits.text: A proposal alone cannot establish which recommendations the company implemented. The 1998 settlement concerned separate litigation.

cases.title: The Panama Papers
cases.question: How did a cross-border publication reach the European Parliament?
cases.summary: Investigative reporting, a public company database and a parliamentary inquiry produced different kinds of evidence. Follow the dates from the first stories to Parliament’s recommendations.

sources.title: Panama Papers investigation and frequently asked questions
Release of searchable offshore company data
Recommendation following the inquiry into money laundering, tax avoidance and tax evasion
About the Offshore Leaks Database

timeline.title: The first stories appear
timeline.text: ICIJ and its partners published their first coordinated reports based on records from the law firm Mossack Fonseca.

timeline.title: A public subset becomes searchable
timeline.text: ICIJ opened company data covering nearly 214,000 offshore entities across 21 jurisdictions.

timeline.title: Parliament adopts recommendations
timeline.text: After its inquiry, the European Parliament issued recommendations to the Council and Commission, including stronger supervision and cooperation.

finding.text: ICIJ released structured information about offshore entities and their connections. The public database contains a selection from the underlying reporting material.

outcome.text: The published parliamentary recommendation records what Parliament called for. Its conclusions concern the application of EU law and weaknesses in oversight.

limits.text: An offshore entity may have legitimate uses. A listing alone cannot establish misconduct or tax liability, and the public database omits many underlying records.

connection.title: Explore the Offshore Records Atlas
connection.text: Compare how places appear in five ICIJ investigations and follow the roles documented in individual records.

cases.title: The Pentagon Papers
cases.question: What changed between the newspaper case and full public release?
cases.summary: A Supreme Court ruling allowed newspaper publication to continue in 1971. Forty years later the US National Archives released the complete government study.

sources.title: The Pentagon Papers, official study and volumes
New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U.S. 713
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States via the Library of Congress

sources.title: Announcement of complete Pentagon Papers release

timeline.title: The study is commissioned
timeline.text: Defense Secretary Robert McNamara commissioned a study of US involvement in Vietnam.

timeline.title: The Supreme Court rules
timeline.text: The government sought orders preventing the New York Times and Washington Post from printing material from the study. The Court ruled against the government.

timeline.title: The complete study is released
timeline.text: The National Archives made the report and its supporting documents available in full. Compared with the earlier Gravel edition, the Archives counted about 2,384 pages newly opened to the public.

finding.text: The Court held that the government had failed to meet the burden required to justify prior restraint in these cases. The separate opinions give the justices’ different reasons.

outcome.text: Readers can open individual volumes of the approximately 7,000-page official release and compare the material with the narrower publication dispute.

limits.text: The 1971 decision concerns the requested orders against two newspapers. It does not resolve every legal question about obtaining or publishing classified information.

cases.title: WikiLeaks and the Assange plea
cases.question: What did the 2024 guilty plea actually decide?
cases.summary: The public record distinguishes WikiLeaks’ wartime publications from the specific offence Julian Assange admitted in federal court in Saipan.

sources.title: United States v. Julian Assange, plea agreement
sources.publisher: US District Court for the Northern Mariana Islands via the US Department of Justice

sources.title: Announcement of guilty plea and sentence

timeline.title: Wartime documents are published
timeline.text: WikiLeaks published material concerning Iraq and Afghanistan and US diplomatic communications. These publications form part of the historical background described by the Department of Justice.

timeline.title: The parties reach a plea agreement
timeline.text: The written agreement sets out a single conspiracy count and the parties’ agreed position on sentence.

timeline.title: The court imposes sentence
timeline.text: Assange pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands. The court sentenced him to time served, reflecting 62 months spent in custody in the United Kingdom.

finding.text: The plea concerned conspiracy to obtain and disclose national defense information. The signed agreement identifies the offence and distinguishes the parties’ commitments from the court’s sentencing decision.

outcome.text: The court imposed a sentence of time served. The Department of Justice announced the result on 25 June on the US mainland, when it was already 26 June in Saipan.

limits.text: A plea resolves the identified charge against one defendant. It supplies no judicial finding about the accuracy of every published document or the legality of other publishers’ work.
